hints: Focus on the big risk for animal cells in culture: they have only a fragile cell surface membrane and no cell wall, so what happens if water rushes in or out?
Think about water potential and osmosis: how would matching the salt concentration outside the cell to the inside stop any net gain or loss of water?
walkthrough:
**Spot the vulnerability of animal cells**

Hello, great thinking here. Animal cells have no cell wall to support them.

If too much water enters by osmosis they burst, and if too much leaves they shrivel. Both will kill them.

**Recall what controls water movement**

Water always moves by osmosis from higher water potential (more dilute) to lower water potential (more concentrated).

The salt solution sets the water potential outside the cells.

**Choose an isotonic solution to keep cells stable**

We make the salt solution isotonic, meaning it has the same water potential as the cytoplasm.

$$\text{no water potential gradient} \rightarrow \text{no net osmosis}$$ 
So there is no net movement of water in or out, and the cells stay alive.

options.A: Facilitated diffusion of some ions does happen, but that is not why we add the bathing solution. The main job is to balance water.
options.B: Ions can still diffuse in and out through channels and pumps. The solution does not and cannot stop all ion movement.
options.C: Correct. An isotonic salt solution matches the cell contents, so there is no net osmosis and the cells neither burst nor shrink.
options.D: Salts do not supply energy. Energy for active transport comes from ATP made in respiration, not from the surrounding solution.
